events.label: A private search specialist said his team had not located Bulley in a specified section of river.
Police said two people had been arrested on suspicion of malicious communications; the reported bail and custody statuses were provisional procedural states.
The Independent published former-detective commentary at 06:50 GMT, before the police press conference; this was not a police update.
At a press conference police described Bulley’s risk classification and addressed speculation, followed by disclosure of limited personal information.
Police announced recovery of a body from the River Wyre; formal identification had not yet taken place.
Police confirmed the recovered body was Nicola Bulley; the family statement criticized speculation and media approaches and asked for privacy.
Ofcom said it had written to Sky and ITV seeking explanations after the family’s complaints; this was a request for information, not a breach finding.
The PCC announced a College of Policing review; the force also referred its prior contact to the IOPC, which later confirmed the referral date and investigation scope.

Those possibilities are guest claims, not established findings. Date basis: hosting_page_publication. The publisher page's article publication time is not an aired time. Search-accessible page evidence shows a play control and describes interview content, but no player duration or linear broadcast log was recovered. The hypothetical kidnapping claim is not verified by this record. Only the Faulding player is identified here; the neighbour quotation is not a second recovered clip.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: Our strongest defence is that these updates followed distinct public developments rather than simply repeating a missing-person alert. On 8 February, a private search specialist described an area his team had checked; that was an attributed observation, not a police conclusion. The recovered 14 February page records two arrests on suspicion of malicious communications and the reported procedural status. On 15 February, police addressed speculation and disclosed limited personal information. The archive confirms the 14 February account; later police material explains the official position. Those dates and sources belong in the story because readers needed to distinguish a search account, an arrest update and an official briefing.

That defence has limits. Former specialists’ theories and police descriptions can attract attention without resolving what happened. A careful report should label expert comment as opinion, explain the basis for police statements, and avoid turning absence of information into a claim. Later identification or review findings cannot be projected backwards as facts known to readers that week. The sample does not show every editorial decision, every contact with the family or the full wording and prominence of every item. It also cannot establish that coverage caused harm. Our case is about what these dated items added, not a claim that every choice was justified.

Compared with the other selected reporting, this strand is strongest where it gives a verifiable new status and weakest where commentary risks outrunning evidence. The family’s later request to stop speculation is a necessary counterpoint; it should prompt restraint, not be treated as proof of a specific breach. The archive lookup was partial, and a failed check of one incorrect URL says nothing about other snapshots. These records support a limited defence of timely updates, alongside a clear obligation to correct uncertainty and avoid repeating unsupported theories.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: The clearest defence is that these reports tracked several genuinely different developments. On 16 February, the family asked people to stop speculation while the search was still under way. On 19 February, police said a body had been recovered but identification was pending. On 20 February, police confirmed the identity and the family issued a further statement criticizing speculation and media approaches. Then, on 21 February, Ofcom said it had written to two broadcasters seeking explanations. A recovery, an identification, a family response and a regulator’s request each changed what the public could responsibly know. Reporting them on separate dates helps readers follow that sequence rather than collapse it into one event.

The counterargument is serious: the family had asked for privacy and criticized direct approaches, so news value does not excuse intrusive contact or unnecessary personal detail. The Ofcom letter was an information request, not a decision that rules had been breached. The family’s criticism is their account and must remain attributed; it is not itself a regulatory finding. Later reviews also need their own dates and sources. A headline can record timing and emphasis, but this sample cannot reveal every approach made, the full prominence of each report, or the experience of the family.

Against the other selected coverage, this sequence has public value when it clearly marks what changed between 19, 20 and 21 February. It becomes repetitive if it merely recycles grief or speculation without new verified information. The strongest editorial defence is therefore narrow: establish the recovery, wait for formal identification, carry the family’s response with care, and describe Ofcom’s next step precisely. These records support that chronology, not a blanket claim that every story or contact was justified, and they provide no basis for claiming that reporting caused the death.

briefing.title: A fictional desk defence of its sampled coverage

paragraphs.text: A reasonable defence is that these selected items moved between different kinds of information: a 9 February search update, former detectives’ recommendations published early on 15 February, criticism of police disclosure, and later oversight news. The expert article appeared at 06:50 GMT, before the police press conference that day, so it should be understood as commentary in the developing search, not a response to the briefing. On 22 February, the review announcement and the IOPC referral concerned separate processes. That distinction matters: a review being commissioned is a new procedural development, but it is not a final finding about police conduct.

The counterargument is that lists of possible clues can amplify speculation, particularly when a family is living through a search and has asked for privacy. Former detectives’ suggestions do not establish that police missed a line of inquiry or that any theory was true. Nor does later oversight prove that every earlier report was wrong. A careful defence must acknowledge the duty to minimize personal detail, label professional commentary, and separate it from confirmed fact. The selected records cannot show the full article treatment, all editorial choices or how readers responded, and they do not establish harm or causation.

Compared with straight police updates, the expert piece offered interpretation rather than a new verified fact; compared with later oversight coverage, the 22 February announcement marked a process beginning, not its conclusion. The fairest account recognizes both public interest in examining search decisions and the risk of presenting conjecture as discovery. Subsequent official findings must be identified as retrospective and were unavailable to readers in this window. Four sampled records are too few to characterize the whole desk. They support a limited defence of covering distinct stages, paired with restraint where additional detail would only feed uncertainty.

context.statusAtWindowEnd: Use only the minimum verified public facts about Nicola Bulley. Attribute police statements, private specialist views, family statements and unverified online claims. The recovery was announced on 19 February and identification confirmed on 20 February. Ofcom’s explanation request was not a breach finding. Later official review findings are retrospective; do not claim reporting caused the death.

sequence.text: A private search specialist said his team had not located Bulley in a specified section of river.
Police said two people had been arrested on suspicion of malicious communications; the reported bail and custody statuses were provisional procedural states.
The Independent published former-detective commentary at 06:50 GMT, before the police press conference; this was not a police update.
At a press conference police described Bulley’s risk classification and addressed speculation, followed by disclosure of limited personal information.
Police announced recovery of a body from the River Wyre; formal identification had not yet taken place.
Police confirmed the recovered body was Nicola Bulley; the family statement criticized speculation and media approaches and asked for privacy.
Ofcom said it had written to Sky and ITV seeking explanations after the family’s complaints; this was a request for information, not a breach finding.
The PCC announced a College of Policing review; the force also referred its prior contact to the IOPC, which later confirmed the referral date and investigation scope.

retrospectiveEvidence.text: The College of Policing later assessed the investigation and communication. Its finding that the personal-information disclosure was avoidable and unnecessary is retrospective and was not available during the February window.

publicContext.intro: Nicola Bulley disappeared in Lancashire in January 2023. Public coverage moved from search updates and speculation to scrutiny of police communication and later oversight. A body was recovered on 19 February and identified as Bulley on 20 February. Consider when reporting added verified public information and whose decisions warranted scrutiny.
publicContext.allegationResponse: Use minimal personal detail. Attribute family criticism and distinguish it from regulatory findings. The College review is retrospective; this sample does not attribute Bulley’s death to reporting.

accountabilityRecords.limit: This is a dated procedural update, not an upheld breach. No later final merits decision was recovered in this research pass; that gap does not establish that none exists.

accountabilityRecords.title: An independent review examines the disclosure
accountabilityRecords.summary: The independent review concluded that releasing personal information on 15 February was avoidable and unnecessary, and examined police communications under intense news and social-media attention.
accountabilityRecords.limit: The review assesses the police response; it is not a legal finding against each publisher or a complete count of online speculation. Personal health details are not repeated here.

accountabilityRecords.title: Communication changes reported to the Accountability Board
accountabilityRecords.summary: The Deputy Chief Constable reported that all but two actions from the review were complete. Media-engagement training and a peer review remained outstanding.
accountabilityRecords.limit: These are recorded progress claims by the organisations involved, not an independent implementation audit or proof that wider media practices changed.

accountabilityScope.rule: Later findings have their own dates and scope. They are excluded from the headline counts and do not establish what an editor knew at first publication. An institution’s account, a reported finding and a court judgment are different kinds of evidence.
accountabilityScope.gaps: Samples remain uneven. Complete daily social reach, full broadcast transcripts, earlier page versions and a consistently measured comparator have not been recovered for every case.
